planting.note: Set potted divisions or bare rhizomes into heavy garden soil in an aquatic planting basket, positioning the crown at or just below the water surface at a pond shelf or bog edge in spring; prefers full sun to light shade and steady standing water.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in heavy loam within a submerged aquatic container so the crown sits under one to two inches of water, or in permanently saturated soil at the pond margin. Give the plant full sun to light shade and avoid letting the container dry out during the growing season. In early summer it sends up violet-blue, flattened iris blooms with yellow throat markings above narrow, sword-shaped foliage, making it a graceful marginal accent distinct from the more aggressive yellow flag iris. It spreads slowly by rhizome and rarely self-sows aggressively, so it is a good choice where a well-behaved marginal iris is wanted.

planting.note: Plant the knobby tuber in a submerged aquatic basket of heavy loam set 12 to 24 inches below the water surface so the strap-like leaves float freely on top; thrives in cool water and full sun to light shade.

directions: Set the tuber horizontally in a wide aquatic planting basket filled with heavy garden soil, then lower the container to a depth of one to two feet so the oblong leaves reach the surface and float. It performs best in cool water and can be grown in ponds that ice over lightly in winter, provided the tuber stays below the freeze line. Forked spikes of fragrant, vanilla-scented white flowers with black anthers appear mainly during cooler months, often blooming in fall and again in spring when most water lilies are dormant. The floating foliage also offers shade and cover for fish, making it a useful companion plant in mixed water gardens.

planting.note: Plant nursery-propagated divisions in a container of live sphagnum moss and coarse sand kept constantly wet with cool, mineral-free water; site where roots stay cool and the pitchers get bright light, ideally with running or seeping water through the pot.

directions: Grow only nursery-propagated stock in a bog container or pond-edge planting of live sphagnum moss, perlite, and sand, watered exclusively with rain, distilled, or reverse-osmosis water since it is sensitive to minerals and fertilizer. Its distinctive tubular, hooded pitchers resemble a rearing cobra and are veined with translucent patches that lure and trap insects for the plant's nutrition. Unlike most Sarracenia, it needs consistently cool root temperatures, so situating the pot where cold water can trickle through or keeping it partly shaded from hot afternoon sun helps it thrive. It is a striking, conversation-starting addition to a shaded bog garden or the cool margin of a water feature.

common_name: Perry's Fire Opal Water Lily (Hardy Orange-Red Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant the tuberous rootstock horizontally in a wide aquatic container of heavy clay loam topped with pea gravel, then submerge so the crown sits 6 to 18 inches below the water surface in a sunny, still section of the pond.

directions: Set the rootstock in a wide planting basket of heavy garden soil capped with gravel to keep it in place, then lower the pot so the growing crown rests six to eighteen inches beneath the surface in full sun. This hardy Perry D. Slocum hybrid was bred for its unusually warm coloring among hardy lilies, opening a fiery orange that deepens toward red-orange as each flower ages. Star-shaped blooms sit just above rounded green pads from late spring through fall, with a moderate spread that suits small to mid-sized garden ponds and large tubs. Regular removal of spent flowers and yellowing pads keeps the plant blooming steadily through the season.

common_name: Escarboucle Water Lily (Classic Marliac Crimson-Red Hardy Water Lily)

planting.note: Set the rhizome horizontally in a wide planting basket of heavy garden soil capped with gravel, then lower the container so the crown rests 12 to 24 inches beneath the water surface in full sun.

directions: Anchor the rhizome in a wide aquatic basket of heavy loam topped with gravel, then submerge the container so the crown sits one to two feet below the surface in full sun. This vigorous, century-old French hybrid from the Latour-Marliac nursery produces large, brilliant crimson-red flowers with prominent golden stamens that stay open even in partly shaded or cooler water where many other lilies close early. Bloom runs from early summer into fall, and the dark green pads spread generously, so it suits medium to large ponds better than small container water gardens. It is widely regarded as one of the most reliable and free-flowering red hardy water lilies available.

common_name: Colorado Water Lily (Changeable Apricot-Pink Hardy Water Lily)

planting.note: Plant the tuber in an aquatic basket of heavy loam topped with gravel and submerge so the crown sits 8 to 18 inches below the surface in a sunny, calm spot.

directions: Position the tuber in a container of heavy garden soil topped with gravel and lower it into the pond so the crown rests eight to eighteen inches below the water surface in full sun. This hardy changeable-type lily is prized for flowers that open a warm salmon-apricot and gradually deepen to a coppery pink as they age, giving multiple color tones on the plant at once. The lightly tea-scented blooms are held just above mottled bronze-green pads from late spring through fall. Its moderate spread makes it a good fit for mid-sized backyard ponds where a color-shifting bloom is wanted without overwhelming the water surface.

common_name: Gonnère Water Lily (Classic Marliac Double White Water Lily)

planting.note: Set the rootstock in a wide container of heavy garden soil topped with pea gravel and lower it so the crown rests 8 to 18 inches below the water's surface in full sun.

directions: Plant the rootstock in a heavy loam and gravel-topped aquatic basket, then submerge it so the crown sits eight to eighteen inches beneath the surface in a sunny, calm part of the pond. Another classic introduction from the historic Latour-Marliac nursery, it produces fully double, camellia-like pure white flowers with a light fragrance that open nearly flat above rounded green pads. Bloom continues from early summer to fall, and the compact, floriferous habit makes it well suited to small and medium ponds or large half-barrel water gardens. Its crisp white flowers pair well as a contrast plant alongside darker-colored or yellow-flowered lily cultivars.

common_name: Baby Doll Lotus (Dwarf White Bowl Lotus)

planting.note: Plant the tuber horizontally just beneath the soil surface in a wide, shallow container of heavy clay loam, then set the pot so 2 to 4 inches of water covers the soil in a sunny, warm, wind-sheltered spot.

directions: Lay the tuber horizontally just under the soil surface in a wide, shallow tub of heavy clay loam, being careful not to break the growing tip, then top the container with two to four inches of water in a warm, sheltered, sunny spot. This is one of the smallest lotus cultivars available, staying compact enough for a half-barrel or large tub rather than requiring a full-sized pond. It produces small, creamy-white single blooms held on short stems above rounded blue-green leaves once the water has warmed in early summer, continuing intermittently into fall. Its dwarf scale makes it a popular choice for patio water gardens and for gardeners wanting to try lotus culture without dedicating a large pond to it.

common_name: King Tut Umbrella Papyrus (Dwarf Egyptian Papyrus)

planting.note: Grow in a submerged aquatic pot of heavy garden soil set so the crown and lower stems sit 1 to 6 inches underwater at the pond's edge, or in consistently saturated soil beside the water; move indoors before frost outside zone 9-11.

directions: Set potted divisions into a submerged aquatic container of heavy garden soil so the crown and lower stems sit an inch or two underwater along the pond's edge, or grow it in a large container of constantly saturated soil. This selection of Egyptian papyrus is more compact and sturdier-stemmed than the straight species, forming tall, leafless stalks topped with dense, mop-like umbels of thin, drooping bracts that catch the breeze. It does not flower showily but is grown for its bold vertical texture and architectural silhouette at the water's edge. Outside its hardy range it is typically grown as a warm-season annual or overwintered indoors as a houseplant with the pot kept in a saucer of water.

common_name: Kermesina Blue Flag Iris (Wine-Red Native Iris Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions of the rhizome in heavy soil at the pond margin or in a submerged container so the crown sits at or just below the waterline, in full sun to light shade.

directions: Set rhizome divisions into heavy garden soil at the pond edge or in a submerged aquatic container so the crown rests at or just below the waterline, choosing a spot with full sun to light shade. This selection of the native blue flag iris produces richly saturated wine-red to magenta-purple flowers with yellow-and-white signal markings in late spring, held above upright, sword-shaped foliage. Like the wild species, it tolerates both shallow standing water and consistently moist soil, spreading gradually by rhizome without becoming aggressive. It offers a deeper, moodier color option than the typical blue-violet species for pond margins, rain gardens, and native plant bog plantings.
